evaluation.positioning_hook: A laid-off ex-Marine and a doorman-turned-thief are forced into an uneasy alliance when a crooked cop frames them both, turning a wrong-number feud into a violent conspiracy hunt.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clear, commercial engine: two combustible guys, a corrupt-cop conspiracy, and escalating violence. The challenge is that the script’s heavy reliance on racial insult comedy and abrasive banter narrows the audience even as the cat-and-mouse setup broadens it.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The wrong-number inciting incident is immediate and easy to explain, and the story keeps converting that premise into bigger complications. The hook is clear, though the conspiracy layer takes a while to fully reveal itself.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jake and Deshon are distinct, contradictory, and built for friction, especially once their Marine background and shared resentment surface. But both are defined more by attitude and insult rhythm than by deeper emotional specificity for much of the script.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar home-invasion/corruption thriller lane and gives it a racially charged, two-hander verbal duel as its engine. That’s a bold surface choice, but the underlying conspiracy beats are more familiar than the premise initially suggests.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating through break-ins, surveillance, planted evidence, and shifting alliances, with each turn forcing the characters into a new tactical move. The momentum is strongest in the middle stretch, where the cat-and-mouse mechanics keep tightening.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The wrong-number setup plus the eventual reveal that the antagonists are corrupt cops gives the script a clean, memorable spine. The execution is less singular than the premise, because many of the reversals land in recognizable thriller territory.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The script builds a specific working-class ecosystem: used-car lots, apartment lobbies, pool halls, back-alley payoffs, and a corrupt chain of command. That texture gives the story a lived-in, street-level feel and makes the conspiracy feel embedded in a real social world.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistently abrasive, macho, and darkly comic, with a strong insult-driven rhythm. It’s specific, but the repeated racial slur exchanges can flatten tonal variety and make the script feel one-note over time.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in the Marine history, the men’s lost ambitions, and the corrupt system around them. But the script mostly keeps those ideas at the level of functional backstory rather than letting them deepen the emotional stakes.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jake/Deshon is the engine, and the supporting web around them—Ronnie, Molloy, Haley, Kendra, Buck, Sargoza—creates recurring pressure points. The relationships generate story well, especially once alliances start shifting and everyone has leverage on everyone else.

lead_characters.name: Jake Corelli
lead_characters.demographics: White male, mid-30s, ex-Marine, working-class, average-to-good-looking, physically solid.
lead_characters.hook: Jake is a laid-off used-car salesman with a soldier’s reflexes and a hair-trigger ego, the kind of guy who turns humiliation into a mission. He starts as a smart-mouthed lone wolf, then gets pushed into survival mode when he realizes the wrong-number feud is actually a setup. His arc is less about becoming brave than about learning who to trust when his instincts keep making the situation worse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young Bruce Willis in Die Hard or a tougher, more combustible Josh Brolin-type turn: a guy who can sell cocky banter, physical confidence, and panic under pressure in the same scene. The role gives an actor a full-body escalation from smug control to wounded survival.

lead_characters.name: Deshon Dunn
lead_characters.demographics: Black male, mid-30s, ex-Marine, amputee with a prosthetic lower leg, working-class, physically imposing.
lead_characters.hook: Deshon is a doorman, thief, and fast-talking hustler who weaponizes attitude to stay ahead of the people using him. He’s funny, dangerous, and more disciplined than he first appears, with the prosthetic leg and Marine background giving him a hard-earned physical and emotional edge. He’s the script’s most surprising presence because he starts as the antagonist and becomes the story’s most pragmatic survivor.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael K. Williams in The Wire or Mahershala Ali in Moonlight a chance to play intelligence, menace, humor, and pain without ever begging for sympathy. It’s a performance part with swagger, vulnerability, and a strong physical signature.

lead_characters.name: Ronnie Dyson
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-40s, physically intimidating, police officer, corrupt, working-class.
lead_characters.hook: Ronnie is the smiling predator in a badge, the guy who can move between uniformed authority and street-level intimidation without changing his temperature. He’s the story’s most dangerous institutional face because he never looks frantic; he looks like he’s already won. The role plays as calm menace with a bureaucratic cover story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is classic character-actor villain territory in the vein of Bryan Cranston in Drive or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom: controlled, conversational, and quietly terrifying. It gives an actor the pleasure of playing power as routine.

lead_characters.name: Haley
lead_characters.demographics: Black female, late 30s to early 40s, apartment-building employee, working-class.
lead_characters.hook: Haley is smart, sexually self-possessed, and morally compromised in a way that feels practical rather than melodramatic. She’s not just a side player; she’s the bridge between the petty theft world and the police corruption scheme, which makes her both useful and disposable. Her scenes carry the script’s best sense of transactional survival.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actress do what Regina King did in If Beale Street Could Talk or Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country: play intelligence, heat, and danger without losing control of the room. It’s a sharp supporting showcase with real edge.

lead_characters.name: Officer Molloy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, police officer, corrupt, authoritative.
lead_characters.hook: Molloy is the polished institutional enforcer who can smile through a lie and make it sound procedural. She’s less flamboyant than Ronnie, which makes her more unsettling; she’s the one who can turn a complaint into a trap. The role functions as the script’s cold, competent face of corruption.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the clipped authority of Robin Wright in House of Cards or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers: controlled, unreadable, and quietly lethal. It’s a strong power-role with a clean, playable exterior.

lead_characters.name: Buck
lead_characters.demographics: White male, mid-30s to 40s, large, tattooed, redneck/biker presentation.
lead_characters.hook: Buck is the volatile local brute whose rage keeps turning the story physical. He’s less a full character than a recurring threat vector, but he’s memorable because he keeps re-entering the plot as the embodiment of the neighborhood violence Jake can’t outrun. He gives the script a blunt-force antagonist with a nasty streak.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor go full animal in the tradition of Walton Goggins in Justified or Michael Shannon in a smaller, meaner register. It’s a bruising, scene-stealing part built on threat and volatility.

lead_characters.name: Sargoza
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 50s to 60s, judge, authoritative, well-connected.
lead_characters.hook: Sargoza is the polished legal face of the conspiracy, the man who can speak in measured tones while moving people like inventory. He’s important because he reveals the corruption isn’t just street-level; it has institutional cover. The role gives the story a higher-level villain with real procedural authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the gravitas of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Tom Wilkinson in Michael Clayton: controlled authority with rot underneath. It’s a prestige-supporting turn with menace in the restraint.

lead_characters.name: Kendra
lead_characters.demographics: Black female, early 40s, office worker, Deshon’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: Kendra is the practical family anchor who keeps Deshon tethered to ordinary life even as his criminal world closes in. She’s not flashy, but she matters because she gives Deshon a human stake and a reason not to disappear. Her scenes add domestic pressure and a sense of consequence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that gives an actress the family-pressure realism of S. Epatha Merkerson in Chicago Med or Alfre Woodard in Clemency. It’s a credible, emotionally functional part rather than a showy one.

lead_characters.name: Davey
lead_characters.hook: Davey is the awkward outside man Jake uses to tail Deshon, and his presence gives the story a low-rent surveillance texture. He’s not deep, but he’s useful because he shows how desperate Jake has become and how amateur the counter-moves are. He functions as a pressure valve and a plot device with a face.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a character actor play nervous competence in the vein of Paul Giamatti’s smaller, twitchier work or Richard Kind in a darker register. It’s a compact, scene-specific showcase.

casting_characteristics: One amputee role requiring a prosthetic lower leg
Several roles depend on strong physical presence and regional dialect/color
Two principal male roles require sharp comic timing and credible menace

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic screen inserts and simple practical coverage.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, blood hits, practical bruising, a prosthetic leg continuity beat, and a few fight sequences.

rights_flags.detail: Miles Davis - 'Kind of Blue' is specifically named on the page.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: mid-budget theatrical or streaming-original crime thriller with adult language, violence, and corruption themes.

budget.note: Contemporary, mostly practical locations, no VFX load, and no large-scale set pieces; the main cost drivers are night exteriors, multiple company moves, and a few fight/shooting scenes.

casting.note: The lead pair needs actors who can sell rapid-fire insult comedy, physical intimidation, and eventual alliance without losing credibility. Deshon also requires an amputee performer or a carefully managed prosthetic solution.

development.note: The script’s strongest commercial engine is the Jake/Deshon rivalry, but the repeated racial insult exchanges and the late conspiracy reveal create a buyer conversation about tone and audience reach.

comp_set.title: Cop Land
comp_set.why_it_comps: Working-class corruption thriller with a local-law-enforcement conspiracy and a protagonist trapped inside a system that protects its own.

comp_set.title: Training Day
comp_set.why_it_comps: Street-level cop corruption, escalating intimidation, and a lead forced to navigate a predator in uniform.

comp_set.title: The Nice Guys
comp_set.why_it_comps: Two mismatched men with sharp banter and escalating danger, where the relationship itself becomes the engine.

comp_set.title: Blue Ruin
comp_set.why_it_comps: A revenge-and-survival thriller built on grimy realism, bad decisions, and a protagonist who keeps getting in deeper.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like hard-edged crime thrillers with combustible male chemistry, corrupt-cop intrigue, and a strong street-level voice.
audience_target.demographics: Mostly 25-54, male-skewing but with real crossover for viewers who respond to character-driven crime stories and antihero banter.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, modest cast, practical action, and no VFX-heavy sequences keep this in indie-feature territory.

types_of_buyers: streamer genre execs building adult crime slates
indie financiers looking for contained commercial thrillers
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult, profanity-forward crime stories where the hook is as much the relationship chemistry as the plot mechanics. The corrupt-cop angle gives it a clean commercial spine, while the two-hander friction makes it castable and trailer-friendly.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the Jake/Deshon dynamic is strong, but there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond this single conspiracy.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has an immediately pitchable engine that can sell in one sentence and get a buyer to the next page. That makes it attractive to producers looking for a contained commercial hook with built-in escalation. The audience for this is anyone who likes a premise that starts small and turns dangerous fast.
strengths.evidence: The opening phone calls between Jake and Deshon turn a mistaken identity into a threat exchange within the first pages.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Jake/Deshon chemistry is the asset.
strengths.what_it_means: The script’s biggest commercial moat is the two-hander friction: insult comedy, mutual suspicion, then reluctant alliance. That gives the project trailer moments, actor bait, and a clear reason for audiences to keep watching. Buyers chasing male-driven crime thrillers will see the casting upside immediately.
strengths.evidence: Their repeated phone duels, the eventual Marine reveal, and the restaurant scene where they finally reset the relationship.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The corrupt-cop conspiracy gives the story scale.
strengths.what_it_means: What begins as a personal feud expands into a broader institutional threat, which raises the stakes without requiring a huge budget. That makes the script more marketable than a simple home-invasion revenge piece because it can play as both character piece and conspiracy thriller. Streamers and genre buyers tend to respond to that kind of escalation.
strengths.evidence: Ronnie, Molloy, Sargoza, and the planted evidence reveal a layered corruption chain.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels lived-in and shootable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script is built out of practical, recognizable locations that give it texture without forcing expensive production design. That keeps the project in a buyer-friendly budget lane and makes it easier to attach a director who wants a grounded crime movie. It’s the kind of world that feels bigger than its footprint.
strengths.evidence: Used-car lot, apartment lobbies, pool hall, alleys, modest homes, and a judge’s office all recur as story spaces.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Deshon is a breakout supporting role.
strengths.what_it_means: The character has enough swagger, contradiction, and physical specificity to attract a strong actor and elevate the package. That matters because a memorable second lead can materially improve buyer interest and festival/streaming visibility. Casting directors will notice the role as a showcase part.
strengths.evidence: Deshon’s prosthetic leg, Marine background, hustler instincts, and eventual tactical intelligence.

whats_special.headline: This is a castable, contained crime thriller with a clean hook, a strong two-hander engine, and a corrupt-cop conspiracy that expands the stakes without expanding the budget. The combination of street-level texture and actor-friendly roles makes it a realistic indie or streaming buy for a buyer building out the adult genre lane.

items.area: The racial insult engine is a buyer sensitivity.
items.detail: A large share of the dialogue is built on repeated slurs and racial provocation between Jake and Deshon. That gives the script its bite, but it also narrows the buyer pool and creates a real tonal conversation about whether the material reads as satirical, incendiary, or simply abrasive.

items.area: The conspiracy reveal arrives in layers.
items.detail: The script spends a long stretch on the wrong-number feud before fully clarifying the corrupt-cop machinery underneath it. That’s workable, but it means the buyer has to trust the escalation before the larger engine is completely visible.

items.area: Jake and Deshon are strongest as attitude, not depth.
items.detail: Both leads are highly playable, but much of their identity is carried by banter, posture, and antagonism rather than deeper interiority. That keeps the script moving, but it limits the emotional lift if the project is being positioned as more than a genre ride.

items.area: The supporting villains are functional, not singular.
items.detail: Ronnie, Molloy, Sargoza, and Buck all serve the plot, but none of them is written with the kind of singularity that would make the antagonistic side of the movie feel iconic. For a buyer, that means the package lives or dies more on the lead chemistry than on a standout villain role.

issues.headline: The main friction is tonal: the script’s most distinctive voice comes from repeated racial provocation, which is also the element most likely to limit the buyer pool. Beyond that, the movie is built to move, but it asks the audience to stay with attitude and escalation more than with deep character revelation.
